message:
Please review the following document.

<document>
Post-Implementation Review: Automated Triage for Home Insurance Claims
Claims Operations, Harrowgate Mutual, September 2026

1. Summary
In March 2026 we introduced automated triage for home insurance claims. Claims under £1,500 that pass a set of automated checks are fast-tracked for straight-through settlement, without review by a claims handler. This review compares five months before launch (October 2025 to February 2026) with five months after (April to August 2026), with March excluded as a transition month, and recommends next steps.

2. How the triage works
When a claim is notified online or by phone, the system checks policy cover, excess, claim history and a set of rules covering the type and circumstances of loss. Claims under the £1,500 threshold that pass all checks are paid within 48 hours. All other claims, and any claim flagged by a rule, are allocated to a handler as before. Fast-tracked claims are not reviewed by the fraud screening team, which previously sampled low-value claims manually.

3. Results
Table 1. Before and after comparison (monthly averages)
Measure | Before (Oct-Feb) | After (Apr-Aug)
Claims received per month | 4,200 | 4,350
Share of claims fast-tracked | 0% | 38%
Average days to settle, all claims | 14.2 | 9.8
Customer satisfaction (post-claim survey, 0-100) | 71 | 79
Handler hours per month | 9,600 | 7,900
Fraud referrals per 1,000 claims | 6.1 | 3.9

Average settlement time fell by 4.4 days, a 38% improvement. Customer satisfaction rose eight points, the largest movement we have recorded in a single year. Handler hours fell by 1,700 a month, or about 18%, allowing us to absorb higher claim volumes and reduce agency staff usage over the summer.

Fast-tracked claims averaged £740. Complaints about the fast-track route were few and related mainly to customers whose claims were declined by the automated checks and who felt they had not been given a reason.

The triage rules were developed with the claims technical team and tested against 18 months of historical claims before launch. In that testing, the rules would have fast-tracked 36% of historical claims, close to the 38% seen in live operation, which gives us confidence that the rules are behaving as designed. No changes to the rules were needed after go-live.

4. Financial impact
At a fully loaded handler cost of £31 an hour, the reduction of 1,700 handler hours a month saves about £52,700 a month, or £632,400 a year. System licence and maintenance costs are £140,000 a year, giving a net annual saving of around £492,000.

5. Fraud context
The Special Investigations Unit's 2025 annual report found that claims between £1,500 and £3,000 make up 22% of home claim volume but 41% of confirmed fraud cases, with false or inflated contents claims the most common type. Claims under £1,500 accounted for 14% of confirmed fraud cases.

6. Recommendations
6.1 Raise the fast-track threshold from £1,000 to £3,000 from January 2027. We estimate this would increase the share of claims fast-tracked from 38% to around 55%, saving a further 1,100 handler hours a month, about £409,000 a year at current rates, and extending faster settlement to many more customers.
6.2 Give customers whose claims are declined by the automated checks a clear explanation and a direct route to a handler.
6.3 Review the automated rules quarterly with the claims technical team.
6.4 Publish the fast-track service standard on our website so that customers know what to expect when they make a claim.

7. Conclusion
Automated triage has delivered faster settlement, higher satisfaction and lower handling costs, with a net saving of nearly half a million pounds a year. Extending it to claims up to £3,000 is the natural next step and would substantially increase the benefit to customers and the business.
</document>
response:
# Review: Automated Triage Post-Implementation Review

The results are encouraging, but the recommendation to extend to £3,000 isn't supported by the evidence presented. The main problem is that the review does not measure fraud leakage, and the proposal moves into the highest-risk claim band.

## Major issues

**1. The fraud evidence points against the recommendation.**
- Section 5 says claims of £1,500-£3,000 are 22% of volume but 41% of confirmed fraud. That is the band 6.1 would fast-track, and fast-tracked claims get no fraud screening (Section 2).
- Fraud referrals fell from 6.1 to 3.9 per 1,000 (-36%). The review does not comment on this, and the likeliest explanation is that fraud is no longer being looked at, not that it has declined. The manual sampling of low-value claims has stopped.
- The financial case (Section 4) has no line for fraud leakage. Without it, the £492k net saving is overstated by an unknown amount.
- Testing showed the rules fast-track a similar share of claims (36% vs 38%). That shows the rules fire as expected, not that they catch fraud. "No changes needed" is not evidence of accuracy.

**2. The threshold is inconsistent.** Section 2 says the current threshold is £1,500. Recommendation 6.1 says it will be raised "from £1,000". One of these is wrong, and the size of the proposed increase (and the 38% to 55% estimate) depends on which. The basis for the 55% and 1,100-hour estimates also isn't shown.

**3. The before/after comparison is confounded.** The "before" period is October to February and the "after" period is April to August. Claim type, volume, and complexity are seasonal (winter storms, escape of water, freezing), so some of the improvement in settlement time, handler hours, and satisfaction may not come from triage. There is no control or seasonal adjustment, such as comparing with the same months a year earlier.

## Numerical errors and weak claims

- **"4.4 days, a 38% improvement" is wrong.** 4.4 / 14.2 is about 31%. The 38% appears to have been confused with the fast-track share.
- The other figures check out: 18% handler hours reduction (17.7%), £52,700 a month, £632,400 a year, £492,400 net, and £409,200 for the extension.
- Back-solving the settlement figures (fast-track at about 2 days) implies non-fast-tracked claims still take about 14-15 days. The gain comes entirely from the fast-tracked claims, which are probably the simplest ones anyway. The "all claims" average slightly overstates the improvement.
- "Largest movement we have recorded in a single year" is unsupported, and the survey may be affected by the mix of claims. Fast-tracked customers are the ones likely to be happy.
- Handler-hour savings are presented as cash savings. They are cashable only if the hours were actually removed, for example through reduced agency use. The review should show that.

## Other inconsistencies and gaps

- Section 2 says flagged claims go to a handler, but Section 3 refers to claims "declined by the automated checks". Which is it? If the system can decline claims automatically, that is a significant fairness and regulatory issue (for example Consumer Duty and fair treatment), and not just a complaints point. The review should say how many claims are declined and whether there is any appeal.
- No data is given on the number of complaints, overpayments, or reopened claims.
- Recommendation 6.3 (quarterly rule review) is fine, but it sits oddly with "no changes needed", and no performance metrics are named for it.

## Suggested changes before this goes forward

1. Correct the 38% figure to about 31%, and reconcile the £1,000 / £1,500 threshold.
2. Add a fraud analysis covering confirmed fraud rates on fast-tracked claims, a retrospective sample audit of fast-tracked claims by the SIU, and an estimate of leakage in £.
3. Reinstate some fraud sampling of fast-tracked claims, and make it a precondition of any extension.
4. Add a seasonally adjusted comparison (year-on-year).
5. Phase the extension (for example to £2,000 first, with monitoring) instead of going directly to £3,000, and tie the financial case to leakage-adjusted figures.
6. Clarify the decline process and how it is explained to customers.

If fraud leakage in the £1,500-£3,000 band is even a modest share of claims paid, it could erase much of the £409k extension saving.
